Beyond Prediction Residuals: Conformal Regret Calibration for Robust Contextual Linear Optimization

Lingjie Zhao    Hansheng Jiang    Wei Qi
Abstract

Predict-then-optimize systems convert contextual forecasts into decisions, yet conformal robust optimization typically calibrates prediction residuals rather than downstream loss. For linear optimization, this parameter-space geometry can be badly misaligned with decision risk: large objective perturbations may preserve the optimizer, while small boundary-crossing perturbations may cause substantial regret. We introduce Conformal Regret Sets, a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that conformalizes an optimization-derived regret surrogate and uses its calibrated level set for minimax-regret refinement. We first show that directly conformalizing exact regret, although sufficient to certify the nominal predict-then-optimize decision, yields a degenerate robust problem: absent an exogenous bounded support, every alternative decision has unbounded worst-case regret. We therefore use SPO+, a pointwise upper bound on exact regret, as the conformal score, obtaining distribution-free finite-sample marginal regret guarantees under exchangeability. For contextual linear programs, the resulting set decomposes into polyhedral pieces aligned with the normal fan of the feasible polytope. A vertex is active if and only if its predicted suboptimality gap is at most half the calibrated threshold η\eta, enabling local, output-sensitive generation of all relevant pieces. Moreover, if Γ\Gamma is the predicted gap to the closest competing vertex, the nominal and refined decisions admit the sharper worst-case-regret certificate (η−2​Γ)+(\eta-2\Gamma)_{+}, with an exact early exit when η≤2​Γ\eta\leq 2\Gamma. Experiments on contextual fractional knapsack validate the geometry and certificates: continuous refinement reduces the 0.950.95-quantile and CVaR0.95\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.95} of regret by 9.1%9.1\% and 13.1%13.1\% relative to nominal PTO, while vertex-restricted refinement changes only 10.0%10.0\% of nominal decisions.

2Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto

1 Introduction

Predictive models are increasingly embedded in downstream optimization systems. In the standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) pipeline, observable features are mapped to uncertain problem parameters, and the resulting point prediction is inserted into a deterministic optimization problem. This modular paradigm is natural for contextual linear programs (LPs) arising in routing, allocation, and portfolio selection (Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis 1998; Bertsimas and Kallus 2020). Yet a point forecast alone offers no protection against prediction error, and optimizing an estimated objective can amplify modest errors into substantial post-decision loss (Smith and Winkler 2006).

A common remedy is to replace the point prediction with a data-driven uncertainty set and solve a robust optimization problem. Conformal prediction (CP) is attractive for this purpose because it is model-agnostic and provides distribution-free, finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability (Angelopoulos and Bates 2023). Existing conformal approaches to contextual optimization typically calibrate residual scores, such as coordinatewise errors or norm distances between predicted and realized objective vectors (Sun et al. 2023; Patel et al. 2024). The resulting boxes, ellipsoids, or norm balls are statistically valid in parameter space, but need not be aligned with downstream decision risk.

For an LP, residual coverage is not decision calibration. The objective space is partitioned by the normal fan of the feasible polytope: all costs in one cone select the same optimal vertex. A large perturbation can remain within a cone and incur no decision loss, whereas a smaller perturbation can cross a nearby boundary, change the optimizer, and cause substantial regret. Some directions also shift every feasible objective value equally and are therefore irrelevant to both the optimizer and pairwise regret. Residual-based scores do not distinguish these decision-invariant directions from decision-sensitive ones. This leads to the following question: Can conformal uncertainty instead be calibrated directly in units of downstream regret while still supporting nontrivial robust re-optimization?

Conformal validity alone is not the obstacle: the score sublevel set must also support meaningful comparison of alternative actions. The most direct score is exact decision regret, or the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss (Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022). Although its conformal quantile immediately certifies the nominal PTO decision, we prove that, without an independently imposed bounded objective support, its sublevel set is degenerate for re-optimization: every alternative decision has infinite worst-case regret. Thus, a score that is ideal for certifying one fixed action can be unusable for comparing actions.

We therefore introduce Conformal Regret Sets based on SPO+, a pointwise upper bound on exact regret. Split-conformal calibration produces a threshold η\eta in objective-value units, yielding a finite-sample marginal regret guarantee and an objective-space set for minimax-regret refinement. The construction is post hoc and compatible with any black-box predictor. For contextual LPs, the SPO+ level set has an exact normal-fan structure that makes this otherwise nonconvex robust problem analyzable and amenable to output-sensitive solution methods.

Our contributions are threefold.

  • •

    Regret calibration and the need for a robustifiable score. We formalize conformal calibration with optimization regret, establish the degeneracy of exact-SPO sublevel sets for robust refinement, and show that SPO+ calibration provides a distribution-free finite-sample guarantee for the regret of the nominal PTO decision.

  • •

    Exact normal-fan geometry and local active-set generation. We derive a closed polyhedral representation of the SPO+ conformal regret set, exact whenever the hindsight optimizer is unique, and show that its unbounded directions are decision-invariant. A vertex generates a nonempty piece if and only if its predicted suboptimality gap is at most η/2\eta/2. These active vertices form a connected subgraph of the polytope’s one-skeleton, enabling output-sensitive generation from the nominal solution rather than enumeration of all vertices.

  • •

    Margin-certified minimax-regret refinement. Let Γ\Gamma be the predicted gap between the nominal optimizer and its closest competing vertex. We prove that the certified worst-case regret of the nominal, vertex-restricted, and continuous refinements is at most (η−2​Γ)+(\eta-2\Gamma)_{+}. With η=ηα\eta=\eta_{\alpha}, the same bound controls realized regret with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha. Hence η≤2​Γ\eta\leq 2\Gamma gives a zero worst-case-regret certificate over the calibrated set and an exact early-exit test. Otherwise, adjacency-based generation and a fixed-piece LP oracle evaluate the regret adversary without enumerating all comparator vertices; once the active pieces are generated, the continuous refinement admits a finite LP formulation.

2 Related Work

Conformal prediction for optimization. CP provides distribution-free prediction regions under exchangeability (Angelopoulos and Bates 2023), and a growing literature uses these regions as uncertainty sets for contextual robust optimization (Zhao et al. 2026). Early methods primarily calibrate parameter-space errors, including ellipsoidal sets (Johnstone and Cox 2021), residual-based sets for contextual LPs (Sun et al. 2023), and generative, potentially nonconvex regions (Patel et al. 2024). Conformal ideas have also been combined with inverse optimization and adherence-aware prescription (Chan et al. 2024). More broadly, conformal risk control extends conformal guarantees beyond miscoverage to generic monotone losses (Angelopoulos et al. 2024).

Decision-aware conformal score design. Beyond residual calibration, recent work makes uncertainty quantification for optimization more decision-aware. End-to-end conditional robust optimization trains predictive and uncertainty models using downstream decision loss (Chenreddy and Delage 2024), while conformal methods learn calibrated convex or polyhedral set geometry from the induced robust loss (Yeh et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2026). In particular, Chen et al. (2026) learn geometry within a parameterized polyhedral family and then recalibrate on independent data. Utility-directed CP incorporates a user-specified downstream utility into conformal score design (Cortes-Gomez et al. 2025); Hu et al. (2026) design sets under explicit robustness constraints, and Zhou and Zhu (2026) calibrate downstream robustness levels. CREDO combines conformal and inverse-optimization geometry to audit the probability that a fixed candidate decision is suboptimal (Zhou et al. 2026). Our construction derives set geometry directly from the optimization-based SPO+ score. The resulting nonconvex, normal-fan-aligned sets admit exact active-piece screening, margin-adaptive certificates, and certified minimax-regret refinement for contextual LPs.

Smart predict-then-optimize and decision-focused learning. Decision-focused learning (DFL) addresses the mismatch between prediction accuracy and downstream performance by differentiating through, or otherwise exploiting, the optimization problem during training (Donti et al. 2017; Wilder et al. 2019; Mandi et al. 2022; Gupta and Huang 2024). The Smart PTO framework uses decision regret as the training objective and introduces SPO+ as a tractable convex surrogate for linear optimization (Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022). Liu and Grigas (2021) study surrogate-risk calibration, relating excess SPO+ risk to excess expected SPO risk to support predictor learning. Subsequent work develops optimization-aware losses and training procedures across linear, combinatorial, probabilistic, and causal settings (Qi et al. 2025; Berden et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2025); robust-constraint-aware training is considered through the SPO-RC loss (Im et al. 2025). Our calibration is post hoc: we apply split-conformal calibration to SPO+ scores from a fixed predictor, obtaining finite-sample marginal coverage and regret guarantees for minimax-regret refinement.

3 Problem Setup and Regret Calibration

3.1 Contextual Linear Optimization and Decision Regret

Consider a linear program (LP) that takes the following standard form:

min\displaystyle\min c⊤​x,\displaystyle\ c^{\top}x, (1)
s.t. A​x=b,x≥0,\displaystyle\ Ax=b,x\geq 0, (2)

where x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the decision variable, c∈ℝnc\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the uncertain parameter, and A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and b∈ℝmb\in\mathbb{R}^{m} (m≤nm\leq n) define the deterministic system constraints. We assume throughout that 𝒳:={x∈ℝn:Ax=b,x≥0}\mathcal{X}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:Ax=b,\ x\geq 0\} is a nonempty compact polytope. Let 𝒱:=ext⁡(𝒳)={v1,…,vK}\mathcal{V}:=\operatorname{ext}(\mathcal{X})=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{K}\} be its complete set of distinct geometric vertices, and write [K]:={1,…,K}[K]:=\{1,\ldots,K\}. For any realized cost vector cc, let x∗​(c)∈arg⁡minx∈𝒳​c⊤​xx^{*}(c)\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}c^{\top}x be a fixed deterministic measurable vertex-valued optimal selector. Throughout the main text, we assume that every cost vector under consideration induces a unique optimizer, so the selector is immaterial there; tie-boundary extensions are treated in the appendix.

For a feasible decision x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and a realized objective vector cc, define its decision regret as

Reg⁡(x,c):=c⊤​x−c⊤​x∗​(c).\operatorname{Reg}(x,c):=c^{\top}x-c^{\top}x^{*}(c). (3)

It measures the excess realized cost of xx relative to the hindsight optimum and is therefore nonnegative.

In the Predict-Then-Optimize paradigm, a predictor f^:ℝd→ℝn\hat{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} maps observable features zz to a point estimate c^\hat{c} of the uncertain parameter cc. The PTO simply prescribes x∗​(c^)x^{*}(\hat{c}), but the fragility of decisions based on point forecasts motivates robust methods, i.e., replacing c^\hat{c} with an uncertainty set and optimizing against its worst-case realization.

3.2 Split Conformal Calibration

To quantify predictive uncertainty, we leverage split conformal prediction (Angelopoulos and Bates 2023). Let 𝒟c​a​l={(zi,ci)}i=1N\mathcal{D}_{cal}=\{(z_{i},c_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} be a held-out calibration sample set, and define a conformal score function s⁡(z,c)s(z,c) measuring the discrepancy between the prediction f^​(z)\hat{f}(z) and the realization cc. Evaluating this score on 𝒟c​a​l\mathcal{D}_{cal} yields empirical scores 𝒮={si}i=1N\mathcal{S}=\{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and the order statistics s(1)≤⋯≤s(N)s_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq s_{(N)}. For a target miscoverage level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), set

qα:=⌈(N+1)​(1−α)⌉,ηα:=s(qα),q_{\alpha}:=\left\lceil(N+1)(1-\alpha)\right\rceil,\qquad\eta_{\alpha}:=s_{(q_{\alpha})}, (4)

with s(N+1)=+∞s_{(N+1)}=+\infty. For any new test instance zz, the conformal uncertainty set is constructed as the level set

𝒰α​(z)={c∈ℝn:s⁡(z,c)≤ηα}.\mathcal{U}_{\alpha}(z)=\left\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:s(z,c)\leq\eta_{\alpha}\right\}. (5)

Under the standard exchangeability assumption, the foundational result in conformal prediction yields a distribution-free finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee,

ℙ⁡(ctest∈𝒰α​(ztest))≥1−α.\mathbb{P}(c_{\mathrm{test}}\in\mathcal{U}_{\alpha}(z_{\mathrm{test}}))\geq 1-\alpha.

The choice of score determines the geometry and downstream meaning of the resulting set. We next specialize the score to decision-aware optimization settings.

3.3 SPO+ Conformal Regret Set and Optimization

Existing conformal robust optimization methods typically calibrate generic parameter-space sets, such as norm balls, boxes, ellipsoids, and budgeted sets. Although these sets admit well-established deterministic reformulations, they often ignore downstream decision geometry. This mismatch motivates constructing uncertainty sets by directly calibrating decision regret. For the nominal PTO decision, the natural score is its realized regret, namely the exact SPO loss (Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022):

sSPO​(c,c^)=c⊤​x∗​(c^)−c⊤​x∗​(c).s_{\text{SPO}}(c,\hat{c})=c^{\top}x^{*}(\hat{c})-c^{\top}x^{*}(c). (6)

For any threshold η≥0\eta\geq 0, define the SPO uncertainty set as

𝒰SPO​(c^,η):={c∈ℝn:sSPO​(c,c^)≤η}.\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO}}(\hat{c};\eta):=\left\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:s_{\mathrm{SPO}}(c,\hat{c})\leq\eta\right\}. (7)

By construction, every c∈𝒰SPO​(c^,η)c\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO}}(\hat{c};\eta) certifies that the nominal PTO decision incurs regret at most η\eta. However, this fixed-decision certificate does not necessarily provide a useful uncertainty representation for selecting alternative prescriptions: as the following proposition shows, regret-robust refinement over the exact-SPO uncertainty sets is degenerate.

Proposition 1 (Degeneracy of exact-SPO refinement).

Suppose that 𝒳\mathcal{X} contains at least two distinct points and that x^:=x∗​(c^)\hat{x}:=x^{*}(\hat{c}) is a vertex of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For every finite η≥0\eta\geq 0,

supc∈𝒰SPO​(c^,η)Reg⁡(x^,c)≤η,\sup_{c\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO}}(\hat{c};\eta)}\operatorname{Reg}(\hat{x},c)\leq\eta,

whereas, for every x∈𝒳∖{x^}x\in\mathcal{X}\setminus\{\hat{x}\},

supc∈𝒰SPO​(c^,η)Reg⁡(x,c)=+∞.\sup_{c\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO}}(\hat{c};\eta)}\operatorname{Reg}(x,c)=+\infty.

Consequently, x^\hat{x} is the unique minimizer of the corresponding worst-case regret problem.

Proposition 1 shows that exact SPO is suitable for certifying the nominal PTO decision but cannot support nontrivial refinement: every alternative prescription has infinite worst-case regret over its sublevel set. An independently justified compact objective support can restore boundedness, but this boundedness is supplied externally rather than by the exact-SPO score. Detailed proofs and a comprehensive treatment of the theoretical extensions are provided in the appendix.

This motivates using the SPO+ function for robustification. Unlike the action-specific exact-SPO certificate, SPO+ retains comparator-wise information across alternative decisions. For a realized parameter cc and prediction c^\hat{c}, define

sSPO+​(c,c^)=maxx∈𝒳⁡{(c−2​c^)⊤​x}+(2​c^−c)⊤​x∗​(c),s_{\text{SPO+}}(c,\hat{c})=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\{(c-2\hat{c})^{\top}x\}+(2\hat{c}-c)^{\top}x^{*}(c), (8)

which pointwise bounds the exact regret (SPO function). Applying the split-conformal procedure in Section 3.2 to the SPO+ scores yields the threshold ηα\eta_{\alpha} and the conformal regret set

𝒰SPO+​(c^,ηα)={c∈ℝn:sSPO+​(c,c^)≤ηα}.\mathcal{U}_{\text{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta_{\alpha})=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:s_{\text{SPO+}}(c,\hat{c})\leq\eta_{\alpha}\}. (9)

As formalized below, this construction translates conformal validity into a finite-sample guarantee on the regret of the nominal PTO decision.

Theorem 1 (Finite-sample regret validity).

Let c^test:=f^​(ztest)\hat{c}_{\mathrm{test}}:=\hat{f}(z_{\mathrm{test}}). If the calibration and test observations are exchangeable and the predictor f^\hat{f} is trained on data independent of the joint calibration–test sample, then

ℙ{ctest∈𝒰S​P​O+(c^test;ηα)}≥1−α.\mathbb{P}\!\left\{c_{\mathrm{test}}\in\mathcal{U}_{SPO+}\bigl(\hat{c}_{\mathrm{test}};\eta_{\alpha}\bigr)\right\}\geq 1-\alpha. (10)

Moreover, the nominal PTO decision satisfies

ℙ⁡(ctest⊤​x∗​(c^test)−ctest⊤​x∗​(ctest)≤ηα)≥1−α.\mathbb{P}\left(c_{\mathrm{test}}^{\top}x^{*}(\hat{c}_{\mathrm{test}})-c_{\mathrm{test}}^{\top}x^{*}(c_{\mathrm{test}})\leq\eta_{\alpha}\right)\geq 1-\alpha. (11)

Theorem 1 provides an interpretable operational certificate by bounding the regret of a prescribed action before deployment. In conventional robust optimization, conservatism is controlled through geometric parameters, such as uncertainty-set radii or budgets, whose implications for decision quality may be difficult to interpret. In contrast, our framework links the coverage level 1−α1-\alpha directly to a regret threshold ηα\eta_{\alpha}, allowing practitioners to assess the trade-off between statistical reliability and tolerated suboptimality.

Downstream regret refinement.

The conformal set can also be used to select a decision that is less exposed to adverse objective realizations than the nominal PTO prescription. For any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and a generic threshold η≥0\eta\geq 0, define its worst-case regret over this set as

ρη​(x,c^):=supc∈𝒰S​P​O+​(c^,η)Reg⁡(x,c).\rho_{\eta}(x;\hat{c}):=\sup_{c\in\mathcal{U}_{SPO+}(\hat{c};\eta)}\operatorname{Reg}(x,c). (12)

Given a nonempty compact admissible decision domain 𝒟⊆𝒳\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{X}, the corresponding regret-robust refinement is

x𝒟RR​(c^)∈arg⁡minx∈𝒟​ρηα​(x,c^).x_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RR}}(\hat{c})\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{D}}\rho_{\eta_{\alpha}}(x;\hat{c}). (13)

Later, we consider the two principal choices 𝒟=𝒱\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{V}, which restricts the refinement to feasible vertices, and 𝒟=𝒳\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{X}, which permits any feasible point.

4 Geometry and Regret Refinement

Fix a prediction c^\hat{c} and a threshold η≥0\eta\geq 0, and write ρη​(x):=ρη​(x,c^)\rho_{\eta}(x):=\rho_{\eta}(x;\hat{c}). Because the SPO+ conformal regret set is generally nonconvex, we first exploit its geometry rather than optimize over it monolithically. We first derive a vertex-indexed polyhedral decomposition and establish finite worst-case regret on each piece. We then characterize and locally generate the nonempty pieces, with certified truncation based on predicted gaps. Finally, we develop margin-based certificates and computational formulations for regret refinement without requiring a complete vertex description.

4.1 Polyhedral Decomposition of Set Geometry

Within a region where a fixed vertex vkv_{k} is hindsight optimal, the SPO+ score is convex and piecewise linear in cc, so its sublevel set is polyhedral. The union of these regional sets need not be convex. Under the main-text unique-optimizer assumption, this yields the following exact decomposition; the tie-safe extension is given in the appendix.

Theorem 2 (Polyhedral Decomposition).

At any cost vector cc with unique optimizer vkv_{k},

c∈𝒰SPO+(c^;η)⟺c∈Pk,c\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c\in P_{k},

where

Pk={c∈ℝn:\displaystyle P_{k}=\Bigl\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{n}: c⊤​(vj−vk)≤η+2​c^⊤​(vj−vk),\displaystyle c^{\top}(v_{j}-v_{k})\leq\eta+2\hat{c}^{\top}(v_{j}-v_{k}), (14)
c⊤(vk−vj)≤0,∀j∈{1,…,K}}.\displaystyle c^{\top}(v_{k}-v_{j})\leq 0,\ \forall j\in\{1,\dots,K\}\Bigr\}.

Although ⋃k=1KPk\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}P_{k} additionally includes cost vectors with tied optimizers, it is the closure of the unique-optimizer portion of 𝒰SPO+​(c^,η)\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta) and, by continuity of regret, yields the same worst-case regret values. The second group of inequalities makes vkv_{k} optimal under cc, while the first imposes the SPO+ threshold conditional on vkv_{k} being hindsight optimal. Hence, on PkP_{k}, Reg⁡(x,c)=c⊤​(x−vk)\operatorname{Reg}(x,c)=c^{\top}(x-v_{k}), and worst-case regret can be evaluated piecewise over the union.

An unbounded piece PkP_{k} can still induce finite worst-case regret. The following result characterizes its recession cone rec⁡(Pk)\operatorname{rec}(P_{k}) and the worst-case regret ϕk​(x)\phi_{k}(x) of a feasible decision xx over that piece.

Proposition 2 (Finite regret over each piece).

For every nonempty piece PkP_{k},

rec⁡(Pk)=span⁡(𝒳−𝒳)⟂.\operatorname{rec}(P_{k})=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{X}-\mathcal{X})^{\perp}. (15)

Consequently, for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

ϕk​(x):=maxc∈Pk⁡c⊤​(x−vk)\phi_{k}(x):=\max_{c\in P_{k}}c^{\top}(x-v_{k}) (16)

is finite and attained.

Proposition 2 shows that the ambient unboundedness of PkP_{k} is harmless for regret evaluation: its recession directions are decision invariant, so every active piece induces a finite and attained adversarial problem. Consequently, worst-case regret over the nonconvex set can be evaluated piecewise over the active pieces.

Let

𝒜:={k∈[K]:Pk≠∅}\mathcal{A}:=\{k\in[K]:P_{k}\neq\varnothing\} (17)

denote the active-piece index set. It follows that, for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

ρη​(x)=maxk∈𝒜⁡ϕk​(x).\rho_{\eta}(x)=\max_{k\in\mathcal{A}}\phi_{k}(x). (18)

The decomposition is exact but may still be computationally large: KK can be exponential, and each PkP_{k} in (14) contains constraints indexed by all comparator vertices. The next subsection addresses the first issue through active-piece screening and local generation, while Section 4.3 addresses the second through a constraint-based fixed-piece problem reformulation (oracle).

4.2 Active-Piece Screening and Generation

We first address the number of potential pieces. For each vk∈𝒱v_{k}\in\mathcal{V}, define its predicted gap relative to v^=x∗​(c^)\hat{v}=x^{*}(\hat{c}) as

Δk:=c^⊤​(vk−v^)≥0.\Delta_{k}:=\hat{c}^{\top}(v_{k}-\hat{v})\geq 0. (19)

The following result gives an exact characterization of the nonempty polyhedral pieces.

Theorem 3 (Exact active-piece screening).

For every vertex vk∈𝒱v_{k}\in\mathcal{V} and every finite threshold η≥0\eta\geq 0,

Pk≠∅⟺Δk≤η2.P_{k}\neq\emptyset\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Delta_{k}\leq\frac{\eta}{2}. (20)

Therefore,

𝒜={k∈[K]:Δk≤η2}.\mathcal{A}=\left\{k\in[K]:\Delta_{k}\leq\frac{\eta}{2}\right\}. (21)

The relevant complexity is determined by the number of η/2\eta/2-near-optimal vertices rather than by |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|. It may be much smaller when the nominal optimizer is well separated, although it can remain exponential in the worst case.

Screening alone would still require evaluating Δk\Delta_{k} for every vertex. We next show that the active vertices can be generated locally. Let 𝒢𝒳\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{X}} denote the one-skeleton of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and for any τ≥0\tau\geq 0 define

𝒱τ:={v∈𝒱:c^⊤​(v−v^)≤τ}.\mathcal{V}_{\tau}:=\left\{v\in\mathcal{V}:\hat{c}^{\top}(v-\hat{v})\leq\tau\right\}. (22)
Proposition 3 (Connectivity of predicted near-optimal vertices).

For every τ≥0\tau\geq 0, the subgraph of 𝒢𝒳\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{X}} induced by 𝒱τ\mathcal{V}_{\tau} is connected. More precisely, for every v∈𝒱τv\in\mathcal{V}_{\tau}, there exists an edge path v^=v0,v1,…,vL=v\hat{v}=v^{0},v^{1},\ldots,v^{L}=v such that

c^⊤​v0≤c^⊤​v1≤⋯≤c^⊤​vL,\hat{c}^{\top}v^{0}\leq\hat{c}^{\top}v^{1}\leq\cdots\leq\hat{c}^{\top}v^{L}, (23)

and every vertex on the path belongs to 𝒱τ\mathcal{V}_{\tau}.

Setting τ=η/2\tau=\eta/2, Theorem 3 and Proposition 3 yield a direct local generation procedure. Starting from v^\hat{v}, we enumerate adjacent vertices, retain those satisfying c^⊤​(v−v^)≤η/2,\hat{c}^{\top}(v-\hat{v})\leq\eta/2, and recursively expand every newly retained vertex. Because the induced active subgraph is connected, exhaustive traversal recovers every active piece without expanding an inactive vertex. We call this procedure a margin-truncated adjacency search.

Given an adjacency oracle, the search expands only active vertices while inspecting their incident edges. Its computational effort therefore scales with the explored active subgraph and the oracle cost, rather than with the full vertex set. A best-first search prioritizes vertices by Δ⁡(v):=c^⊤​(v−v^),\Delta(v):=\hat{c}^{\top}(v-\hat{v}), thereby enumerating active vertices in nondecreasing predicted gap and enabling certified early termination.

This ordering also enables a certified early-stopping rule. For 0≤τ≤η/20\leq\tau\leq\eta/2, define the truncated active set and its restricted regret adversary as

𝒜τ\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\tau} :={k∈𝒜:Δk≤τ},\displaystyle:=\{k\in\mathcal{A}:\Delta_{k}\leq\tau\}, (24)
ρη,τ​(x)\displaystyle\rho_{\eta,\tau}(x) :=maxk∈𝒜τ⁡ϕk​(x).\displaystyle:=\max_{k\in\mathcal{A}_{\tau}}\phi_{k}(x).
Corollary 1 (Certified gap-ordered truncation).

For every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the contribution of the omitted active pieces satisfies

maxk∈𝒜∖𝒜τ⁡ϕk​(x)≤Bτ​(x):=(η+2​c^⊤​(x−v^)−2​τ)+,\max_{k\in\mathcal{A}\setminus\mathcal{A}_{\tau}}\phi_{k}(x)\leq B_{\tau}(x):=\left(\eta+2\hat{c}^{\top}(x-\hat{v})-2\tau\right)_{+},

where the maximum over an empty index set is defined as zero.

Let xτ∈arg⁡minx∈𝒟​ρη,τ​(x),Rτ:=ρη,τ​(xτ)x_{\tau}\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{D}}\rho_{\eta,\tau}(x),R_{\tau}:=\rho_{\eta,\tau}(x_{\tau}), and let R𝒟⋆:=minx∈𝒟⁡ρη​(x)R_{\mathcal{D}}^{\star}:=\min_{x\in\mathcal{D}}\rho_{\eta}(x) denote the full refinement value over the same decision domain. Then

Rτ≤R𝒟⋆≤ρη​(xτ)≤max⁡{Rτ,Bτ​(xτ)}.R_{\tau}\leq R_{\mathcal{D}}^{\star}\leq\rho_{\eta}(x_{\tau})\leq\max\{R_{\tau},B_{\tau}(x_{\tau})\}. (25)

Consequently, Bτ​(xτ)≤RτB_{\tau}(x_{\tau})\leq R_{\tau} certifies that xτx_{\tau} is optimal for the full refinement problem.

Corollary 1 turns best-first enumeration into a certified anytime procedure. At any threshold τ\tau, it provides a lower bound RτR_{\tau} on the full optimum and an upper bound max⁡{Rτ,Bτ​(xτ)}\max\{R_{\tau},B_{\tau}(x_{\tau})\} on the full-set regret of the current truncated solution. The search may terminate with a certificate of exact optimality when Bτ​(xτ)≤RτB_{\tau}(x_{\tau})\leq R_{\tau}, or with an approximate certificate when the resulting certified optimality gap falls below a prescribed tolerance.

4.3 Certified Regret Refinement

The connectivity result also yields a locally computable margin certificate. Let Adj⁡(v^)\operatorname{Adj}(\hat{v}) denote the vertices adjacent to v^\hat{v}, and define

Γ:=minv∈𝒱∖{v^}⁡c^⊤​(v−v^)=minv∈Adj⁡(v^)⁡c^⊤​(v−v^).\Gamma:=\min_{v\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\{\hat{v}\}}\hat{c}^{\top}(v-\hat{v})=\min_{v\in\operatorname{Adj}(\hat{v})}\hat{c}^{\top}(v-\hat{v}). (26)

The second equality follows from Proposition 3. Hence, Γ\Gamma is available from the initial adjacency expansion and measures the predicted separation from the closest competing vertex.

We consider two instances of (13): the pure refinement, restricted to vertices, and the continuous refinement over the full feasible polytope:

xpure\displaystyle x^{\mathrm{pure}} ∈arg⁡minx∈𝒱​ρη​(x),\displaystyle\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}}\rho_{\eta}(x), Rpure\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{pure}} :=ρη​(xpure),\displaystyle:=\rho_{\eta}(x^{\mathrm{pure}}), (27)
xcont\displaystyle x^{\mathrm{cont}} ∈arg⁡minx∈𝒳​ρη​(x),\displaystyle\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\rho_{\eta}(x), Rcont\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{cont}} :=ρη​(xcont).\displaystyle:=\rho_{\eta}(x^{\mathrm{cont}}). (28)

For q∈{pure,cont}q\in\{\mathrm{pure,cont}\}, let xtestqx^{q}_{\mathrm{test}} and RtestqR^{q}_{\mathrm{test}} denote the corresponding refined decision and robust regret value at c^test\hat{c}_{\mathrm{test}}.

Theorem 4 (Margin-certified regret refinement).

The two refinement problems attain their optima and satisfy

0≤Rcont≤Rpure≤ρη​(v^)≤(η−2​Γ)+≤η,0\leq R_{\mathrm{cont}}\leq R_{\mathrm{pure}}\leq\rho_{\eta}(\hat{v})\leq(\eta-2\Gamma)_{+}\leq\eta, (29)

where (a)+:=max⁡{a,0}(a)_{+}:=\max\{a,0\}. Moreover, setting η=ηα\eta=\eta_{\alpha}, under the exchangeability condition of Theorem 1,

ℙ{\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\!\Bigl\{ Reg⁡(xtestq,ctest)≤Rtestq\displaystyle\operatorname{Reg}(x^{q}_{\mathrm{test}},c_{\mathrm{test}})\leq R^{q}_{\mathrm{test}}
≤(ηα−2Γtest)+,∀q∈{pure,cont}}≥1−α.\displaystyle\leq(\eta_{\alpha}-2\Gamma_{\mathrm{test}})_{+},\quad\forall q\in\{\mathrm{pure},\mathrm{cont}\}\Bigr\}\geq 1-\alpha.

The deterministic ordering shows that both refinements weakly improve the nominal worst-case certificate, while the larger continuous decision domain cannot perform worse than the vertex-restricted domain. The predicted margin further tightens the calibrated threshold from η\eta to (η−2​Γ)+(\eta-2\Gamma)_{+}. In particular,

η≤2​Γ⟹ρη​(v^)=0.\eta\leq 2\Gamma\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho_{\eta}(\hat{v})=0. (30)

Because Γ\Gamma is available from the initial adjacency expansion, this condition provides an exact early exit: the nominal decision is already certified and refinement is unnecessary. Otherwise, (η−2​Γ)+(\eta-2\Gamma)_{+} quantifies the remaining worst-case certificate. With η=ηα\eta=\eta_{\alpha}, the same bound controls the realized regret of both refinements with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha.

Computational Formulations.

Continuous refinement is natural for fractional or splittable decisions, whereas pure refinement preserves vertex-valued prescriptions. Since 𝒱⊆𝒳,Rcont≤Rpure\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{X},R_{\mathrm{cont}}\leq R_{\mathrm{pure}}; however, this worst-case ordering need not extend to realized mean or tail regret. Moreover, xpurex^{\mathrm{pure}} need not be active, because active vertices index adversarial pieces rather than candidate decisions.

Suppose piece PkP_{k} has constraint matrix HkH_{k} and right-hand-side vector hkh_{k}:

Pk={c∈ℝn:Hk​c≤hk}.P_{k}=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:H_{k}c\leq h_{k}\}. (31)

With nonnegative dual multipliers yky_{k}, strong duality gives

ϕk​(x)=minyk≥0⁡{hk⊤​yk:Hk⊤​yk=x−vk}.\phi_{k}(x)=\min_{y_{k}\geq 0}\left\{h_{k}^{\top}y_{k}:H_{k}^{\top}y_{k}=x-v_{k}\right\}. (32)

Aggregating these dual representations over the active pieces, with a scalar upper bound tt on worst-case regret, yields the following finite continuous master.

Proposition 4 (Finite continuous master).

The continuous refinement value RcontR_{\mathrm{cont}} equals the optimal value of the linear program

minx∈𝒳,t,{yk}k∈𝒜\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathcal{X},\,t,\,\{y_{k}\}_{k\in\mathcal{A}}}\quad t\displaystyle t (33)
s.t. Hk⊤​yk=x−vk,\displaystyle H_{k}^{\top}y_{k}=x-v_{k}, k∈𝒜,\displaystyle k\in\mathcal{A},
hk⊤​yk≤t,\displaystyle h_{k}^{\top}y_{k}\leq t, k∈𝒜,\displaystyle k\in\mathcal{A},
yk≥0,\displaystyle y_{k}\geq 0, k∈𝒜.\displaystyle k\in\mathcal{A}.

Thus, once the active pieces are explicitly represented, continuous refinement reduces to a single linear program whose size depends on the active set.

When the explicit piece descriptions are unavailable or prohibitively large, the original constraint representation of 𝒳={x∈ℝ+n:A​x=b}\mathcal{X}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}:Ax=b\} yields a fixed-piece oracle that avoids all comparator-vertex constraints.

Proposition 5 (Constraint-based fixed-piece oracle).

For any fixed x¯∈𝒳\bar{x}\in\mathcal{X} and active vertex vkv_{k}, ϕk​(x¯)\phi_{k}(\bar{x}) equals the optimal value of

maxc,μ,λ\displaystyle\max_{c,\mu,\lambda}\quad c⊤​(x¯−vk)\displaystyle c^{\top}(\bar{x}-v_{k}) (34)
s.t. A⊤​μ≤c,b⊤​μ=c⊤​vk,\displaystyle A^{\top}\mu\leq c,\qquad b^{\top}\mu=c^{\top}v_{k},
A⊤​λ≥c−2​c^,\displaystyle A^{\top}\lambda\geq c-2\hat{c},
b⊤​λ−(c−2​c^)⊤​vk≤η,\displaystyle b^{\top}\lambda-(c-2\hat{c})^{\top}v_{k}\leq\eta,
μ,λ∈ℝm.\displaystyle\mu,\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.

Here μ\mu and λ\lambda are dual variables for the hindsight minimization and the maximization in the SPO+ score, certifying optimality of vkv_{k} under cc and the SPO+ threshold, respectively. At a master incumbent (x¯,t¯)(\bar{x},\bar{t}), an optimizer ck⋆c_{k}^{\star} of (34) yields the valid cut t≥ck⋆⁣⊤​(x−vk)t\geq c_{k}^{\star\top}(x-v_{k}) whenever ck⋆⁣⊤​(x¯−vk)>t¯c_{k}^{\star\top}(\bar{x}-v_{k})>\bar{t}.

Hence, Propositions 4 and 5 are complementary: explicit pieces yield a single LP, whereas the oracle supports constraint generation for either the continuous or vertex-restricted master directly from (A,b)(A,b). Combined with screening and adjacency generation, they avoid monolithic optimization over the nonconvex conformal set.

5 Experiments

We evaluate the proposed framework using an illustrative example and contextual fractional-knapsack experiments, focusing on set geometry, finite-sample validity, decision performance, and certified active-piece generation.

5.1 Illustrative Geometry of Calibrated Sets

We consider a two-dimensional decision problem with feasible set 𝒱\mathcal{V} given by the eight vertices of a regular octagon and objective minv∈𝒱⁡c⊤​v\min_{v\in\mathcal{V}}c^{\top}v after cc is realized. In Figure 1, each point c=(c1,c2)c=(c_{1},c_{2}) denotes a possible ground-truth cost, while the black cross marks the prediction c^=(−1,−0.35)\hat{c}=(-1,-0.35), which selects the nominal action v^\hat{v}. From left to right, the panels show (i) the hindsight-optimal action for each cc, partitioning cost space into normal-fan regions; (ii) the conventional residual-ℓ2\ell_{2} ball of radius 0.700.70 centered at c^\hat{c}; (iii) the costs for which v^\hat{v} incurs exact regret at most 1.101.10; and (iv) the conformal regret set with SPO++ score at the same illustrative threshold, with colors identifying its active normal-fan pieces. The comparison illustrates both the piecewise-convex structure of the SPO+ set and why only predicted near-optimal vertices need to be generated.

5.2 Experiments on the Fractional Knapsack Problem

Following Ho-Nguyen and Kılınç-Karzan (2022), we generate nonlinear context-dependent item values with multiplicative noise and use their negatives as minimization costs. Complete implementation details are provided in the appendix. Small instances permit exhaustive geometric validation, while larger instances evaluate decision performance and computational efficiency.

Active Pieces and Margin Early Exit

We first use n=8n=8 instances, for which all vertices can be enumerated. Although the feasible polytope contains 320.3320.3 vertices on average, the mean number of active pieces ranges from only 5.335.33 to 1.001.00 across the calibration levels; see Figure 2(a).

The adjacency procedure matches exhaustive enumeration for the active set and second-best margin in all context–level comparisons. At α=0.10\alpha=0.10, all nominal certificates satisfy the margin bound within numerical tolerance, and 30.8%30.8\% of contexts receive a zero certificate (see Theorem 4), allowing the robust master to be skipped. These results validate the exactness and local sparsity of the procedure.

Coverage of Calibrated Sets.

Parameter coverage measures inclusion of the realized cost in the calibrated set; decision-regret coverage measures whether realized regret is bounded by the set-based certificate. Table 1 reports both metrics on the exact n=8n=8 test split, with the decisions for the “Regret set” obtained using continuous regret refinement (RR). Detailed definitions are given in Appendix B.6.

All four methods attain parameter coverage consistent with the nominal levels. The conventional sets nevertheless give essentially 100%100\% decision-regret coverage, which offers little information about decision risk because their full-set regret certificates are substantially wider: parameter inclusion implies decision-regret coverage, whereas the converse need not hold. By contrast, the regret set keeps the two coverage notions more closely aligned, providing a more decision-informative description of uncertainty rather than achieving high coverage through conservative bounds. Complete five-level results and certificate scales are reported in appendix.

Decision Performance against Baselines

We next evaluate decision performance on larger instances with n=20n=20 and α=0.10\alpha=0.10. We compare Nominal PTO with pure and continuous SPO++ regret refinement, as well as conformal Residual-ℓ2\ell_{2}, conformal contextual Box, and KNN–Ellipsoid Cost-RO. Here we follow each method’s intended objective: worst-case cost for RO and minimax regret for SPO+. Adapting the RO baselines to minimax regret goes beyond their standard formulations and can require more involved optimization. To isolate the role of the calibrated set, Appendix B.8 reports objective-matched comparisons, which retain the performance advantage of SPO+ refinement.

Continuous RR provides the strongest tail protection, reducing Q95 and CVaR0.95\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.95} by 9.1%9.1\% and 13.1%13.1\% relative to Nominal PTO, at the cost of higher mean regret. Pure RR changes only 10.0%10.0\% of decisions, remains close to the nominal mean, and achieves the best average performance among all robust methods. These results suggest using PTO when average performance is the priority, Pure RR for selective intervention with limited disruption to nominal decisions, and Continuous RR when upper-tail protection is worth a higher mean regret. Additional experiments on real solar-grid data and sparse transportation LPs are reported in Appendix C.

Certified Early Termination.

We finally evaluate the practical effectiveness of the gap-ordered truncation certificate in Corollary 1 on the main n=20n=20, α=0.10\alpha=0.10 instances. On average, each feasible polytope has 1.16×1061.16\times 10^{6} vertices, of which only 44.9644.96 generate active pieces. Let MM denote the number of generated active pieces. As shown in Figure 3, at M=25M=25, exact optimality is already certified for 99.6%99.6\% of Pure RR and 91.4%91.4\% of Continuous RR instances, although only 56.2%56.2\% of active sets have been fully enumerated. The rates increase to 99.8%99.8\% and 98.4%98.4\%, respectively, at M=50M=50, while both the median and 0.900.90 quantile of the normalized certified gap are already zero at M=25M=25. Thus, the certificate is typically tight enough to establish global optimality well before complete active-set generation. Detailed budget-wise results and runtimes are reported in Appendix B.5.

6 Conclusion

We introduced Conformal Regret Sets, a decision-focused framework that calibrates SPO+ scores to control downstream regret rather than residuals. Split-conformal calibration provides a finite-sample marginal guarantee for the nominal PTO regret, while the induced nonconvex set admits a normal-fan-aligned polyhedral decomposition with exact active-piece screening, local generation, certified truncation, and margin-based certificates. These properties support certified pure and continuous regret-robust refinement without monolithic optimization. Fractional-knapsack experiments validate the theory: pure refinement preserves near-nominal average performance, continuous refinement improves upper-tail protection, and gap-ordered generation often certifies optimality before the full active set is recovered.

A.1 Main Paper

Exact-SPO degeneracy and SPO+ dominance.
Proof of Proposition 1.

The nominal bound is immediate from the definition of the exact-SPO sublevel set. For every c∈𝒰SPO​(c^,η)c\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO}}(\hat{c};\eta),

Reg⁡(x^,c)=c⊤​x^−minu∈𝒳⁡c⊤​u=sSPO​(c,c^)≤η.\operatorname{Reg}(\hat{x},c)=c^{\top}\hat{x}-\min_{u\in\mathcal{X}}c^{\top}u=s_{\mathrm{SPO}}(c,\hat{c})\leq\eta.

Taking the supremum proves the nominal bound in the proposition.

It remains to show that every alternative decision has unbounded regret. Because x^\hat{x} is a vertex of the polyhedron 𝒳\mathcal{X}, it is an exposed point: there exists d∈ℝnd\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that

d⊤​(x−x^)>0for every ​x∈𝒳∖{x^}.d^{\top}(x-\hat{x})>0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal{X}\setminus\{\hat{x}\}. (35)

For completeness, choose dd in the relative interior of the minimization normal cone of x^\hat{x}. The face–normal-cone correspondence for polyhedra states that the minimizers exposed by any vector in this relative interior form exactly the face associated with that normal cone. Since the normal cone is the one associated with the vertex x^\hat{x}, the exposed face is the singleton {x^}\{\hat{x}\}, which proves (35).

For t>0t>0, set ct:=t​dc_{t}:=td. Equation (35) makes x^\hat{x} the unique optimizer under ctc_{t}, and hence

sSPO​(ct,c^)=ct⊤​x^−minu∈𝒳⁡ct⊤​u=0.s_{\mathrm{SPO}}(c_{t},\hat{c})=c_{t}^{\top}\hat{x}-\min_{u\in\mathcal{X}}c_{t}^{\top}u=0.

Thus ct∈𝒰SPO​(c^,η)c_{t}\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO}}(\hat{c};\eta) for every t>0t>0. For any fixed x≠x^x\neq\hat{x},

Reg⁡(x,ct)=t​d⊤​(x−x^)⟶+∞.\operatorname{Reg}(x,c_{t})=t\,d^{\top}(x-\hat{x})\longrightarrow+\infty.

This proves the asserted unboundedness. The robust value at x^\hat{x} is finite, whereas it is infinite at every other feasible decision, so x^\hat{x} is the unique robust minimizer. ∎

We next record explicitly the pointwise inequality used by the conformal argument. Let v:=x∗​(c)v:=x^{*}(c) and v^:=x∗​(c^)\hat{v}:=x^{*}(\hat{c}). Their optimality gives

c⊤​(v^−v)≥0,c^⊤​(v^−v)≤0.c^{\top}(\hat{v}-v)\geq 0,\qquad\hat{c}^{\top}(\hat{v}-v)\leq 0. (36)

=Reg⁡(v^,c)−2​c^⊤​(v^−v)\displaystyle=\operatorname{Reg}(\hat{v},c)-2\hat{c}^{\top}(\hat{v}-v)
≥Reg⁡(v^,c)=sSPO​(c,c^).\displaystyle\geq\operatorname{Reg}(\hat{v},c)=s_{\mathrm{SPO}}(c,\hat{c}). (37)

The last inequality has the stated direction because the second inner product in (36) is nonpositive.

Proof of Theorem 1.

We use the standard split-sample interpretation of the theorem: the training data, and hence the fitted predictor, are independent of the joint calibration–test tuple. Condition on those training data. The fitted predictor and all deterministic measurable optimization maps are then fixed functions, while the calibration and test observations remain exchangeable. Applying the same SPO+ score map to them therefore produces exchangeable scores S1,…,SN,SN+1S_{1},\ldots,S_{N},S_{N+1}. Independence from the calibration sample alone would not suffice if the fitted predictor were allowed to depend on the test observation.

First suppose these N+1N+1 scores are distinct and qα≤Nq_{\alpha}\leq N. The rank RR of SN+1S_{N+1} among all N+1N+1 scores is uniform on {1,…,N+1}\{1,\ldots,N+1\}. Consequently,

ℙ{R≤qα}=qαN+1≥1−α.\mathbb{P}\{R\leq q_{\alpha}\}=\frac{q_{\alpha}}{N+1}\geq 1-\alpha.

If R≤qαR\leq q_{\alpha}, fewer than qαq_{\alpha} calibration scores are smaller than SN+1S_{N+1}, so SN+1≤S(qα)=ηαS_{N+1}\leq S_{(q_{\alpha})}=\eta_{\alpha}. Hence

ℙ{SN+1≤ηα}≥1−α,\mathbb{P}\{S_{N+1}\leq\eta_{\alpha}\}\geq 1-\alpha,

which is exactly (10). When qα=N+1q_{\alpha}=N+1, the convention ηα=+∞\eta_{\alpha}=+\infty makes the inclusion event certain. This last branch is a valid but vacuous statistical statement: all recession, screening, and finite-refinement results below require ηα<+∞\eta_{\alpha}<+\infty. Calibration-score ties are handled without a continuity assumption in the extended analysis below.

On the same score-inclusion event, (37) yields

Reg⁡(x∗​(c^test),ctest)≤sSPO+​(ctest,c^test)≤ηα.\operatorname{Reg}\!\left(x^{*}(\hat{c}_{\mathrm{test}}),c_{\mathrm{test}}\right)\leq s_{\mathrm{SPO+}}\!\left(c_{\mathrm{test}},\hat{c}_{\mathrm{test}}\right)\leq\eta_{\alpha}.

The event on the left therefore has probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, proving the second assertion. ∎

maxμ∈ℝm⁡{b⊤​μ:A⊤​μ≤c}.\max_{\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\{b^{\top}\mu:A^{\top}\mu\leq c\}.

Because vkv_{k} is primal feasible, weak duality implies that the existence of μ\mu satisfying

A⊤​μ≤c,b⊤​μ=c⊤​vkA^{\top}\mu\leq c,\qquad b^{\top}\mu=c^{\top}v_{k}

certifies optimality of vkv_{k} under cc. Conversely, if vkv_{k} is optimal, LP strong duality supplies such a dual-optimal μ\mu.

Next set d:=c−2​c^d:=c-2\hat{c}. Conditional on vkv_{k} being hindsight-optimal, the SPO+ threshold is

maxz∈𝒳⁡d⊤​(z−vk)≤η.\max_{z\in\mathcal{X}}d^{\top}(z-v_{k})\leq\eta. (48)

The dual of max{d⊤z:Az=b,z≥0}\max\{d^{\top}z:Az=b,\ z\geq 0\} is

minλ∈ℝm⁡{b⊤​λ:A⊤​λ≥d}.\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\{b^{\top}\lambda:A^{\top}\lambda\geq d\}.

Nonemptiness and compactness of 𝒳\mathcal{X} make the primal optimum finite and attained, so strong duality shows that (48) holds if and only if there is λ∈ℝm\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{m} such that

A⊤​λ≥c−2​c^,b⊤​λ−(c−2​c^)⊤​vk≤η.A^{\top}\lambda\geq c-2\hat{c},\qquad b^{\top}\lambda-(c-2\hat{c})^{\top}v_{k}\leq\eta.

The μ\mu constraints therefore describe exactly the costs for which vkv_{k} is optimal, while the λ\lambda constraints describe exactly the SPO+ threshold for that same vertex. Their projection onto the cc-coordinates is precisely PkP_{k}. The objective in (34) is c⊤​(x¯−vk)c^{\top}(\bar{x}-v_{k}), so maximizing over the extended formulation has the same value as maximizing over c∈Pkc\in P_{k}, namely ϕk​(x¯)\phi_{k}(\bar{x}). An optimal cc exists by Proposition 2, and strong duality supplies corresponding μ\mu and λ\lambda, so the oracle also attains this value. ∎

A.2 Extended Analysis

Calibration-score ties and the augmented threshold.

The split-conformal guarantee does not require a continuous score distribution. Conditional on training data that are independent of the joint calibration–test tuple, let S1,…,SN,SN+1S_{1},\ldots,S_{N},S_{N+1} be the exchangeable scores. Introduce independent U1,…,UN+1∼Unif⁡(0,1)U_{1},\ldots,U_{N+1}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1) and rank (Si,Ui)(S_{i},U_{i}) lexicographically. These pairs are exchangeable and almost surely distinct, so the rank RR of the test pair is uniform on {1,…,N+1}\{1,\ldots,N+1\}. For qα≤Nq_{\alpha}\leq N,

ℙ{R≤qα}=qαN+1≥1−α.\mathbb{P}\{R\leq q_{\alpha}\}=\frac{q_{\alpha}}{N+1}\geq 1-\alpha.

If SN+1>S(qα)S_{N+1}>S_{(q_{\alpha})}, at least qαq_{\alpha} calibration scores are strictly smaller than SN+1S_{N+1}. Their pairs all precede the test pair, so R>qαR>q_{\alpha}. Taking the contrapositive gives

{R≤qα}⊆{SN+1≤S(qα)}.\{R\leq q_{\alpha}\}\subseteq\{S_{N+1}\leq S_{(q_{\alpha})}\}.

Thus the inclusive conformal event has probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, including when calibration scores are tied.

If qα=N+1q_{\alpha}=N+1, the augmented threshold is +∞+\infty and coverage is one. This is only a vacuous statistical branch. Even when 𝒳\mathcal{X} is compact and every SPO+ score is finite, its +∞+\infty-sublevel set is all of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}; the upper piece inequalities no longer restrict recession directions, and worst-case regret can be infinite. Accordingly, all screening, margin, and finite master results are invoked only when ηα<+∞\eta_{\alpha}<+\infty.

Optimizer ties and the closed piecewise adversary.
Proposition 6 (Tie-safe SPO+ representation and certificates).

Retain the main paper’s unique nominal optimizer v^\hat{v}, but allow realized costs to have optimizer ties and fix any deterministic measurable vertex-valued hindsight selector. For this extension only, define

𝒰¯η:=⋃k=1KPk,ρ¯η​(x):=maxk∈𝒜⁡maxc∈Pk​c⊤​(x−vk).\overline{\mathcal{U}}_{\eta}:=\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}P_{k},\qquad\overline{\rho}_{\eta}(x):=\max_{k\in\mathcal{A}}\max_{c\in P_{k}}c^{\top}(x-v_{k}).

For finite η\eta,

𝒰SPO+​(c^,η)⊆𝒰¯η,\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{U}}_{\eta}, (49)

the two sets agree at every cost having a unique optimizer, and

cl⁡(𝒰SPO+​(c^,η))=𝒰¯η.\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta)\right)=\overline{\mathcal{U}}_{\eta}. (50)

Moreover, for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

0≤ρη​(x)=ρ¯η​(x)<+∞.0\leq\rho_{\eta}(x)=\overline{\rho}_{\eta}(x)<+\infty. (51)

Thus passing to the closed union does not change any worst-case regret value, although it can add boundary costs and ensure that the piecewise adversarial maximum is attained. In particular, every additional cost in 𝒰¯η∖𝒰SPO+​(c^,η)\overline{\mathcal{U}}_{\eta}\setminus\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta) lies on an optimizer-tie boundary.

Define instead a compatible selector as follows: among all vertices minimizing c⊤​vc^{\top}v, first minimize c^⊤​v\hat{c}^{\top}v, and break any remaining tie by a fixed deterministic vertex order. If the SPO+ score and its calibration scores use this same rule, then

𝒰SPO+​(c^,η)=𝒰¯η,ρη​(x)=ρ¯η​(x)for every ​x∈𝒳.\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta)=\overline{\mathcal{U}}_{\eta},\qquad\rho_{\eta}(x)=\overline{\rho}_{\eta}(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal{X}. (52)
Proof.

Take c∈𝒰SPO+​(c^,η)c\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta) and let vk=x∗​(c)v_{k}=x^{*}(c) be the vertex returned by the fixed selector. Its optimality gives c⊤​(vk−vj)≤0c^{\top}(v_{k}-v_{j})\leq 0 for every jj. The score inequality is equivalent to

(c−2​c^)⊤​(vj−vk)≤ηfor every ​j,(c-2\hat{c})^{\top}(v_{j}-v_{k})\leq\eta\qquad\text{for every }j,

which is the upper family defining PkP_{k}. Hence c∈Pkc\in P_{k}, proving (49). If the optimizer under cc is unique, any c∈Pkc\in P_{k} must use that same vkv_{k} in the score, so the upper piece inequalities also prove the reverse inclusion.

The selector-specific set contains 𝒰ηuni\mathcal{U}_{\eta}^{\mathrm{uni}} and is contained in 𝒰¯η\overline{\mathcal{U}}_{\eta}. Taking closures and applying (39) proves (50).

For any c∈Pkc\in P_{k}, the lower inequalities make vkv_{k} optimal even if other vertices are tied. Regret is invariant to which optimizer is used, and therefore

Reg⁡(x,c)=c⊤​(x−vk)for every ​x∈𝒳.\operatorname{Reg}(x,c)=c^{\top}(x-v_{k})\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal{X}. (53)

The regret is continuous in cc, so (50), (53), and Proposition 2 give (51).

It remains to prove exactness of the compatible selector. For a fixed cc, all its optimal vertices share the same value mc:=minj⁡c⊤​vjm_{c}:=\min_{j}c^{\top}v_{j}. Let

M⁡(c):=maxj⁡(c−2​c^)⊤​vj.M(c):=\max_{j}(c-2\hat{c})^{\top}v_{j}.

If vv is any cc-optimal vertex, the SPO+ score obtained by using vv is

M⁡(c)−(c−2​c^)⊤​v=M⁡(c)−mc+2​c^⊤​v.M(c)-(c-2\hat{c})^{\top}v=M(c)-m_{c}+2\hat{c}^{\top}v. (54)

The compatible selector minimizes the final term among all cc-optimal vertices and therefore gives the smallest possible tied-optimizer score. Now take c∈Pkc\in P_{k}. The vertex vkv_{k} is cc-optimal and its upper piece inequalities say that its score is at most η\eta. By (54), the compatible selector has a score no larger than this one, so c∈𝒰SPO+​(c^,η)c\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{SPO+}}(\hat{c};\eta). This proves the reverse inclusion and hence the set equality in (52). The equality of robust values then follows from (53). ∎

For completeness, Proposition 6 also completes the arguments concerning attainment and probability statements under an arbitrary selector. By (51), the selector-specific ρη\rho_{\eta} is the finite maximum of the continuous functions ϕk\phi_{k}, and hence is continuous. It therefore attains a minimum on compact 𝒳\mathcal{X}, while attainment over finite 𝒱\mathcal{V} is immediate. Furthermore,

ρη​(v^)=ρ¯η​(v^)≤(η−2​Γ)+.\rho_{\eta}(\hat{v})=\overline{\rho}_{\eta}(\hat{v})\leq(\eta-2\Gamma)_{+}.

The nested-domain ordering in Theorem 4 therefore holds for the selector-specific refinements as well. On the conformal event, the realized cost belongs to the selector-specific score set by definition, so its regret is bounded directly by the corresponding ρη\rho_{\eta}. Under any deterministic selector, the piecewise representations, truncation bounds, and continuous master compute the exact worst-case value. A closed-piece maximizer may nevertheless be merely a limit point of the selector-specific set; the compatible selector additionally makes the underlying set equality and closed-piece adversarial attainment exact.

Nominal ties, equality boundaries, and singleton polytopes.

Continue to use the closed-union notation introduced above. Suppose now that v^\hat{v} is any fixed vertex selected from a non-singleton optimal face under c^\hat{c}. Then Δk≥0\Delta_{k}\geq 0 still holds for every vertex, and all vertices of the nominal optimal face have zero gap. The graph of a face of a polytope is connected. From v^\hat{v}, first traverse zero-gap edges inside the nominal face as follows. For a target vertex vv, apply the decreasing-edge argument from the proof of Proposition 3 until it terminates at some optimal vertex ww. The nominal face contains both v^\hat{v} and ww, and its one-skeleton gives a zero-gap path from v^\hat{v} to ww. Concatenating this path with the reversal of the descent from vv to ww constructs a nondecreasing path from the selected v^\hat{v} to vv. Hence the induced sublevel graph remains connected without nominal uniqueness.

If the nominal face contains another vertex, the first edge of a path to that vertex has zero gap. Consequently,

Γ=minv∈𝒱∖{v^}⁡c^⊤​(v−v^)=minv∈Adj⁡(v^)⁡c^⊤​(v−v^)=0.\Gamma=\min_{v\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\{\hat{v}\}}\hat{c}^{\top}(v-\hat{v})=\min_{v\in\operatorname{Adj}(\hat{v})}\hat{c}^{\top}(v-\hat{v})=0.

The margin certificate remains valid but reduces to the unstrengthened bound ρ¯η​(v^)≤η\overline{\rho}_{\eta}(\hat{v})\leq\eta.

The inclusive screening boundary is also substantive. If Δk=η/2\Delta_{k}=\eta/2, the witness c=0c=0 keeps PkP_{k} nonempty, while (43) forces c⊤​(v^−vk)=0c^{\top}(\hat{v}-v_{k})=0 throughout the piece. Such a piece may be lower-dimensional. For example, with 𝒳=[0,1]\mathcal{X}=[0,1], c^=1\hat{c}=1, v^=0\hat{v}=0, η=2\eta=2, and vk=1v_{k}=1, its constraints reduce to 0≤−c≤00\leq-c\leq 0, so Pk={0}P_{k}=\{0\}. Likewise, at η=2​Γ<+∞\eta=2\Gamma<+\infty, closest nonnominal pieces are active but (47) forces their regret at v^\hat{v} to be zero. This is why the zero-certificate condition is inclusive.

If |𝒱|=1|\mathcal{V}|=1, define Γ:=+∞\Gamma:=+\infty and, for finite η\eta, (η−2​Γ)+:=0(\eta-2\Gamma)_{+}:=0. There is no nonnominal or adjacent vertex, so the local-neighbor formula is not invoked. Every feasible decision equals v^\hat{v}, every regret and refinement value is zero, and all margin conclusions hold under this convention. If a pure or continuous refinement has multiple minimizers in a nonsingleton problem, every minimizer has the same certificate value; a deterministic measurable tie rule is needed only to make the selected decision a well-defined random variable.

Context-dependent feasible sets and nonpositive costs.

The rank argument remains valid when the feasible polytope varies across observations, provided the full observations

(Zi,Ai,bi,Ci),i=1,…,N+1,(Z_{i},A_{i},b_{i},C_{i}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N+1,

are exchangeable, the training data are independent of this joint tuple, and every realized 𝒳i={x:Aix=bi,x≥0}\mathcal{X}_{i}=\{x:A_{i}x=b_{i},\ x\geq 0\} is nonempty and compact. Assume also that the same jointly measurable optimization and tie-selection maps are used to construct every calibration and test score. Conditional on training, the resulting scores are then exchangeable. All geometric proofs are applied pointwise to each realized polytope. This formulation includes instance-specific prices and capacities in the fractional-knapsack experiments after the usual slack-variable standard-form lifting.

Corollary 2 (Validity with the nonpositive-cost support).

Assume in addition that C∈ℝ−nC\in\mathbb{R}_{-}^{n} almost surely and replace every closed piece by Pk∩ℝ−nP_{k}\cap\mathbb{R}_{-}^{n}. For finite η\eta, exact screening of these supported pieces, finiteness and attainment of piecewise regret, the truncation bound, and the margin certificate remain valid. On the SPO+ conformal event, the realized regret is bounded by the corresponding supported closed-union certificate with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha.

Proof.

The screening necessity argument is unchanged because a supported piece is a subset of PkP_{k}. For sufficiency, the witness c=0c=0 used in (44) also belongs to ℝ−n\mathbb{R}_{-}^{n}, so

Pk∩ℝ−n≠∅⟺Δk≤η/2.P_{k}\cap\mathbb{R}_{-}^{n}\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Delta_{k}\leq\eta/2.

For every nonempty intersection of these polyhedra,

rec⁡(Pk∩ℝ−n)=rec⁡(Pk)∩ℝ−n⊆span⁡(𝒳−𝒳)⟂.\operatorname{rec}(P_{k}\cap\mathbb{R}_{-}^{n})=\operatorname{rec}(P_{k})\cap\mathbb{R}_{-}^{n}\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{X}-\mathcal{X})^{\perp}.

Thus every regret direction x−vkx-v_{k} remains orthogonal to the recession cone, and the finite-generator proof of finiteness and attainment applies unchanged. Intersecting a piece can only decrease its support value, so all truncation and margin upper bounds remain valid.

On the conformal score event, Proposition 6 places CC in a closed piece. The almost-sure sign condition also gives C∈ℝ−nC\in\mathbb{R}_{-}^{n}, so CC belongs to the corresponding supported piece and its realized regret is bounded by the supported closed-union maximum. The event has probability at least 1−α1-\alpha. In the experiments this support condition follows from the construction C=−VC=-V with V≥0V\geq 0. In the fixed-piece oracle, the same intersection is implemented simply by adding c≤0c\leq 0; all other duality constraints are unchanged. ∎

where xjx_{j} is the fraction of item jj selected, pjp_{j} is its price, and bb is the budget. We use a global seed of 42 and deterministic child random streams for the signal matrix and observations. We report one fixed split rather than averages over multiple top-level seeds.

Z∼Unif([0,4]dz),μj(Z)=(Z⊤Θj⋅)2,Z\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,4]^{d_{z}}),\qquad\mu_{j}(Z)=(Z^{\top}\Theta_{j\cdot})^{2},

The optimization models use the minimization-cost convention C=−VC=-V.

Each item price is sampled independently and uniformly from the integers 100 through 1000. Let S=∑jpjS=\sum_{j}p_{j} be the total price and M=maxj⁡pjM=\max_{j}p_{j} the largest item price. With independent U1,U2∼Unif⁡[0,1]U_{1},U_{2}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1], define an upper budget limit b¯\bar{b} and sample bb as follows:

b¯\displaystyle\bar{b} =min{S−10−9,\displaystyle=\min\{S-10^{-9},

b\displaystyle b =M+U2​(b¯−M).\displaystyle=M+U_{2}(\bar{b}-M).

A single deterministic observation stream is generated and then partitioned into disjoint training, calibration, and test subsets. All predictive models are trained on values. Predictions are transformed back to the original value scale and clipped below at zero before conversion to costs. No finite lower bound inferred from the synthetic value distribution is supplied to an uncertainty set.

B.2 Calibration and Evaluation Definitions

For calibration scores S1,…,SncalS_{1},\ldots,S_{n_{\mathrm{cal}}} and miscoverage level α\alpha, the split-conformal threshold is the exact order statistic

kα=⌈(ncal+1)​(1−α)⌉,ηα=S(kα).k_{\alpha}=\left\lceil(n_{\mathrm{cal}}+1)(1-\alpha)\right\rceil,\qquad\eta_{\alpha}=S_{(k_{\alpha})}.

Thus, we do not substitute an interpolated empirical quantile for the conformal order statistic.

Let v⁡(C)∈arg⁡minu∈𝒳⁡(p,b)​C⊤​uv(C)\in\arg\min_{u\in\mathcal{X}(p,b)}C^{\top}u. The SPO++ calibration score is

s+​(C,C^)=maxu∈𝒳⁡(p,b)⁡(C−2​C^)⊤​{u−v⁡(C)}.s_{+}(C,\widehat{C})=\max_{u\in\mathcal{X}(p,b)}(C-2\widehat{C})^{\top}\{u-v(C)\}.

Nominal, hindsight, and SPO++ score problems are solved as linear programs. Optimal-solution ties use a deterministic secondary objective so that the returned solution is a reproducible polytope vertex.

R⁡(x,V,p,b)=maxu∈𝒳⁡(p,b)⁡V⊤​u−V⊤​x.R(x;V,p,b)=\max_{u\in\mathcal{X}(p,b)}V^{\top}u-V^{\top}x.

which assigns exactly 5%5\% empirical probability mass to the upper tail, using fractional weight at a tied boundary when necessary. A decision is recorded as changed when its ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} distance from the nominal PTO decision exceeds 10−610^{-6}.

Exact Enumeration Audit

For every test context, all vertices of the fractional-knapsack polytope are explicitly enumerated. The complete active set obtained by enumeration is compared with the adjacency-based search. The local margin

Γ=minv∈Adj⁡(v^)⁡C^⊤​(v−v^)\Gamma=\min_{v\in\operatorname{Adj}(\widehat{v})}\widehat{C}^{\top}(v-\widehat{v})

B.5 Certified Anytime Active-Piece Generation

We empirically examine the certified early-stopping rule in Corollary 1 under the main n=20n=20, α=0.10\alpha=0.10 setting. The predictor, calibration threshold, and 500500 test contexts are held fixed. The feasible polytopes contain 1.159×1061.159\times 10^{6} vertices on average, while the complete active sets contain only 44.95644.956; the full local traversal evaluates 380.472380.472 distinct vertices on average. For each context, we enumerate active vertices in nondecreasing predicted gap and consider requested prefix budgets

M∈{1,5,10,25,50,100}.M\in\{1,5,10,25,50,100\}.

If the MMth vertex lies on a predicted-gap plateau, the prefix is expanded through the entire plateau. Thus the retained set is exactly 𝒜τ={k:Δk≤τ}\mathcal{A}_{\tau}=\{k:\Delta_{k}\leq\tau\} for the recorded boundary τ\tau; we denote its size by MeffM_{\mathrm{eff}}. This tie-safe convention altered only two of the 500500 contexts at one grid budget each, changing MeffM_{\mathrm{eff}} from 1010 to 1111 and from 2525 to 2727.

For each tie-safe prefix and each decision domain, we solve the restricted refinement and record

Rτ\displaystyle R_{\tau} =ρη,τ​(xτ),\displaystyle=\rho_{\eta,\tau}(x_{\tau}), Bτ\displaystyle B_{\tau} =(η+2​C^⊤​(xτ−v^)−2​τ)+,\displaystyle=\bigl(\eta+2\widehat{C}^{\top}(x_{\tau}-\widehat{v})-2\tau\bigr)_{+},
Uτ\displaystyle U_{\tau} =max⁡{Rτ,Bτ}.\displaystyle=\max\{R_{\tau},B_{\tau}\}.

We declare exact certification only when Bτ≤RτB_{\tau}\leq R_{\tau} up to the prespecified scale-aware tolerance, or when the complete active set has been exhausted. The reported optimality gap is zero in either certified case and Uτ−RτU_{\tau}-R_{\tau} otherwise, normalized by η\eta. As an independent check, every row satisfies Rτ≤R𝒟⋆≤UτR_{\tau}\leq R_{\mathcal{D}}^{\star}\leq U_{\tau}. The reference R𝒟⋆R_{\mathcal{D}}^{\star} is the full-set certificate established in the main experiment: 472472 contexts are exhausted within 100100 pieces, and the separate full-set audit verifies the remaining 2828 contexts.

Figure 3(a) shows that exact certification arrives substantially before exhaustive enumeration. With M=25M=25, the certification rates are 99.6%99.6\% for Pure RR and 91.4%91.4\% for Continuous RR, whereas only 56.2%56.2\% of the active sets have been fully enumerated. At M=50M=50, these rates rise to 99.8%99.8\% and 98.4%98.4\%, respectively; at M=100M=100, they are 100%100\% and 99.8%99.8\%. Equivalently, the first requested grid budget certifying exactness is at most 2525 for 498498 Pure RR instances and 457457 Continuous RR instances. These are first certifying points on the chosen grid, not theoretical minimum prefix sizes.

As shown in Figure 3(b), the certified gap contracts rapidly even before exact termination. For Pure RR, its median is already zero at M=5M=5, while its 0.900.90 quantile falls from 0.7000.700 at M=5M=5 to 0.1280.128 at M=10M=10 and zero at M=25M=25. For Continuous RR, the corresponding median/0.900.90-quantile values are 0.314/0.7390.314/0.739, 0.030/0.3950.030/0.395, and 0/00/0. Hence the gap bound remains informative in the instances that are not yet exactly certified.

Table 3 separates the cost of prefix generation from the robust master. The best-first search takes a median of 15.115.1 ms and a 0.900.90 quantile of 51.851.8 ms by M=100M=100, whereas the paired master solve has corresponding times of 1.0451.045 and 2.9592.959 seconds. Moreover, the median MeffM_{\mathrm{eff}} saturates at 2222, because more than half of the active sets are already complete. These results support the output-sensitive interpretation of the method on this benchmark: a small gap-ordered prefix usually suffices for a rigorous full-problem certificate, and the search itself is not the computational bottleneck.

The single Continuous RR instance not certified by M=100M=100 is a 4,7704{,}770-piece extreme case; its normalized certified gap is 0.1110.111. Thus, rather than recommending M=100M=100 as a general rule, the experiment further supports our conclusion that the number of active pieces required in practice is typically small relative to the total number of vertices.

B.6 Coverage of Calibrated Sets

We compare what the calibrated sets cover in parameter space with what their induced certificates cover at the decision level. This experiment uses the same n=8n=8 split, RBF kernel-ridge predictor, and five calibration levels as the exact-validation experiment. For method mm, let 𝒰m,α​(Zi)\mathcal{U}_{m,\alpha}(Z_{i}) denote its calibrated uncertainty set and let xm,α,ix_{m,\alpha,i} be the decision returned from that set. We record

Im,α,ipar=𝟏{Ci∈𝒰m,α(Zi)}I^{\mathrm{par}}_{m,\alpha,i}=\mathbf{1}\{C_{i}\in\mathcal{U}_{m,\alpha}(Z_{i})\}

and

Im,α,ireg\displaystyle I^{\mathrm{reg}}_{m,\alpha,i} ={Reg(xm,α,i,Ci)≤ρm,α,i},\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{\operatorname{Reg}(x_{m,\alpha,i},C_{i})\leq\rho_{m,\alpha,i}\right\},
ρm,α,i\displaystyle\rho_{m,\alpha,i} =supC′∈𝒰m,α​(Zi)Reg⁡(xm,α,i,C′).\displaystyle=\sup_{C^{\prime}\in\mathcal{U}_{m,\alpha}(Z_{i})}\operatorname{Reg}(x_{m,\alpha,i},C^{\prime}).

The SPO++ row uses the continuous regret-refinement decision. The other three rows use their method-specific Cost-RO decisions, after which ρm,α,i\rho_{m,\alpha,i} is evaluated over the complete corresponding uncertainty set. Thus, the experiment compares the certificates naturally attached to the decisions each method actually prescribes; it does not replace the Cost-RO objectives of the conventional baselines by regret minimization.

As shown in Table 4, parameter coverage generally follows the nominal sequence, with the modest departures expected from one fixed calibration–test split. The largest Bernoulli standard error for 500500 test observations is 0.0220.022, so small differences from 1−α1-\alpha should not be interpreted as evidence for or against the marginal guarantee. More importantly, parameter inclusion deterministically implies decision-regret coverage for every method, but the converse need not hold. The conventional sets consequently attain decision-regret coverage between 0.9920.992 and 1.0001.000, even when their parameter coverage is close to the nominal target. The corresponding gap is smaller for the SPO++ set, especially at the lower miscoverage levels. High decision-regret coverage alone, however, may result from a loose certificate rather than a more informative characterization of decision risk.

To distinguish these explanations, Table 5 reports the scale of the same full-set certificates. The SPO++ certificate has a median of 4.9904.990 at α=.05\alpha=.05 and 1.4071.407 at α=.10\alpha=.10, and its median is exactly zero from α=.20\alpha=.20 onward. Its 0.950.95 quantile falls from 7.6977.697 to zero across the calibration levels. By contrast, the Residual-ℓ2\ell_{2} and KNN–Ellipsoid certificates remain much larger throughout. The contextual box has a slightly smaller median at α=.05\alpha=.05, but its 0.950.95 quantile is 28.94428.944, compared with 7.6977.697 for SPO++. Hence, the near-universal decision-regret coverage of the conventional sets is accompanied by substantially wider regret bounds. This comparison supports the distinction motivating our construction: comparable marginal coverage in parameter space does not by itself imply a decision-informative certificate, whereas calibration in the SPO++ geometry more closely couples coverage to the downstream regret scale. These comparisons concern marginal coverage; they do not assert conditional coverage or uniform dominance in realized decision performance.

B.7 Main Decision-Performance Comparison

Experimental Setup and Refinement Implementation

The main comparison uses

n\displaystyle n =20,dz=15,α=0.10,\displaystyle=20,\qquad d_{z}=15,\qquad\alpha=0.10,
ntrain\displaystyle n_{\mathrm{train}} =5000,ncal=2000,\displaystyle=5000,\quad n_{\mathrm{cal}}=2000,
ntest\displaystyle n_{\mathrm{test}} =500.\displaystyle=500.

All methods use the same observations and test contexts. The principal predictor is polynomial kernel ridge regression, selected by training-only five-fold cross-validation. The tuning grid contains ten logarithmically spaced regularization strengths λ\lambda from 10−310^{-3} to 10310^{3} and polynomial degrees d∈{2,3,4}d\in\{2,3,4\}. The kernel scale is γ=1/dz\gamma=1/d_{z}, and the offset is coef0=1\mathrm{coef0}=1. The selected configuration is degree 22 with λ=2.154\lambda=2.154; its mean cross-validation MSE is 999.114999.114. Feature and multi-output target standardization are fitted inside each training fold, after which the selected model is refitted on all 50005000 training observations.

The compared methods are Nominal PTO, SPO++ Pure RR, SPO++ Continuous RR, Conformal Residual-ℓ2\ell_{2} Cost-RO, Conformal Box Cost-RO, and KNN–Ellipsoid Cost-RO. The two SPO++ methods minimize worst-case regret over the calibrated SPO++ set. Pure RR restricts the returned decision to a vertex of the fractional-knapsack polytope, whereas Continuous RR optimizes over the full fractional polytope.

The active-piece search starts at the nominal vertex and uses a priority queue ordered by the predicted objective gap

δ⁡(v)=C^⊤​(v−v^).\delta(v)=\widehat{C}^{\top}(v-\widehat{v}).

Canonical vertex keys, rounded to ten decimal places, break equal-gap ties. Only vertices satisfying

δ⁡(v)≤η/2+10−9​max⁡{1,|η|}\delta(v)\leq\eta/2+10^{-9}\max\{1,|\eta|\}

are expanded. For computational efficiency, the pure and continuous masters are first solved using the same best-first prefix of at most 100100 active pieces. Every returned decision is then reevaluated against the complete active set, so the reported certificates use the full set rather than the retained prefix. The complete set contains at most 100100 pieces in 472472 of the 500500 test contexts. In each of the remaining 2828 contexts, the full-set certificate is exactly equal to its prefix certificate for both refinements; hence the prefix solution is also optimal for the full active set. The worst-case pieces have maximum prefix ranks 2828 and 2727 for Pure and Continuous RR, respectively. Thus, the 100100-piece limit is only a computational device and does not alter any reported decision or certificate. When η≤2​Γ\eta\leq 2\Gamma, up to the scale-aware numerical tolerance, the nominal decision is returned directly.

Regret-Distribution Profiles

The summary statistics in Table 2 do not identify where the tail benefit of refinement begins. We therefore compare the empirical regret distributions at α=0.10\alpha=0.10 over 100100 evenly spaced quantile levels from 0.500.50 through 0.990.99. Figure 4(a) displays the quantile curves, while panel (b) subtracts the corresponding Nominal PTO quantile to make the location and direction of each difference explicit.

Continuous RR performs worse over the center of the distribution but improves upon Nominal PTO from approximately the 0.940.94 quantile onward, thereby reducing severe regret. Pure RR closely follows the nominal curve and intervenes only in the subset of contexts identified as vulnerable by the calibrated regret model. Hence, continuous refinement emphasizes tail protection, while pure refinement adds robustness with limited disruption to nominal performance.

Pure and Continuous RR are run consecutively with shared active-piece search and model construction; their reported times include this common work and their respective optimization and certification stages.
