Exploratory Results

Table 8 summarizes prediction accuracy, mean decision regret, and complete active-piece counts for the five predictors. The refinement masters use at most the first 150 pieces in best-first order, so this computational cap does not truncate the reported geometric statistic.

Prediction accuracy and downstream performance are related but not interchangeable. Polynomial KRR has the lowest test RMSE (31.5531.55), whereas RBF KRR has the lowest Nominal and Pure-RR mean regrets (7.567.56 and 7.707.70); polynomial KRR instead has the lowest Continuous-RR mean regret (11.1211.12). Pure RR remains close to Nominal PTO for every predictor and slightly improves Ridge from 10.0810.08 to 9.979.97, but is slightly worse for the other four. Continuous RR has higher mean regret than Nominal PTO throughout, consistent with the mean–tail trade-off observed in the main comparison rather than a uniform improvement in average performance. Random forest is weakest in both RMSE and regret, although the remaining prediction and decision rankings are not identical.

Geometric complexity is even less closely related to prediction quality. Polynomial KRR, RBF KRR, and the MLP have similar complete mean active-piece counts (44.9644.96, 45.4745.47, and 45.6645.66), whereas Random Forest has 181.42181.42 and Ridge has the largest mean, 370.63370.63, despite substantially outperforming Random Forest in prediction and decision quality. Margin certificates trigger on only 0.2%0.2\%–0.8%0.8\% of contexts. The 150-piece refinement cap binds in 232 of the 2,500 predictor–context pairs, including 151 Random-Forest pairs; the reported active counts nevertheless use the complete search. These fixed-split comparisons are descriptive: the predictor jointly changes its errors, calibrated score distribution, and local decision geometry, so RMSE alone does not determine regret or search burden.

B.11 Optimization and Numerical Settings

The main knapsack experiments use

OutputFlag\displaystyle\texttt{OutputFlag} =0,Threads=1,\displaystyle=0,\qquad\texttt{Threads}=1,
Seed\displaystyle\texttt{Seed} =42.\displaystyle=42.
MIPGap\displaystyle\texttt{MIPGap} =10−6,\displaystyle=10^{-6},
FeasibilityTol\displaystyle\texttt{FeasibilityTol} =10−7,\displaystyle=10^{-7},
OptimalityTol\displaystyle\texttt{OptimalityTol} =10−7.\displaystyle=10^{-7}.

Fractional-knapsack LPs use deterministic dual simplex and a secondary tie-breaking optimization that preserves the primary objective. The pure vertex master additionally uses IntFeasTol=10−9\texttt{IntFeasTol}=10^{-9}. The auxiliary mixed-integer regret oracle used to evaluate the Cost-RO certificates in Table 5 uses FeasibilityTol=10−9\texttt{FeasibilityTol}=10^{-9} and IntFeasTol=10−7\texttt{IntFeasTol}=10^{-7}. The tighter primal tolerance prevents a feasible-vertex decomposition error from being amplified by the cost coefficients.

The SPO++ masters use constraint generation with at most 200 iterations and add all currently violated cuts at each iteration. The final certificate is independently recomputed over all retained fixed-piece oracles. A solve is accepted only if Gurobi returns OPTIMAL, any applicable relative gap is at most 10−610^{-6}, all certificates are finite, and the normalized physical feasibility residual is at most 10−610^{-6}. The continuous, pure, and nominal certificates must also satisfy their expected hierarchy up to a scale-aware tolerance of 10−610^{-6}. Failures are treated as errors; no failed instance is silently replaced by its nominal decision or removed from the test sample. The Cost-RO decisions themselves use one LP or SOCP and do not optimize through the bilinear adversarial-regret oracle; that oracle is invoked only afterward to evaluate the supplementary full-set certificates.

B.12 Computing Environment

All experiments were run on a PC with an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX processor and 32 GB of RAM, using 64-bit Microsoft Windows 11. The implementation used Python 3.12.7, Gurobi 13.0.1, NumPy 2.4.3, pandas 2.3.2, SciPy 1.16.0, scikit-learn 1.7.1, joblib 1.5.2, and Matplotlib 3.10.6. GPU acceleration is not used. Although the processor provides 24 cores, the main knapsack experiments used one Gurobi thread per solve.

Appendix C Additional Experiments

We complement the fractional-knapsack experiments with two additional LP cases: solar-grid budget allocation using real installation data and synthetic sparse transportation. Both cases compare the same six methods as the main experiment.

C.1 Real-Data Solar-Grid Allocation

Data and Rolling Evaluation Protocol

We follow the solar-grid investment setting of Zhou et al. (2026), using publicly released monthly aggregates of the real solar-installation data studied by Zhou et al. (2025).11 1 attr/Border [0 0 0] user/Subtype /Link /A ¡¡ /S /URI /URI () ¿¿Monthly solar-installation data released with CREDO. The series covers four substations from January 2011–December 2024, with 168168 monthly observations of a four-dimensional count vector and 182182 installations in total. The monthly sequence has no missing observations, and zero-installation months are retained.

For each evaluation year y∈{2013,…,2024}y\in\{2013,\ldots,2024\}, we use a 2424-month window from January of year y−1y-1 through December of year yy. The three chronological splits are:

  • •

    training: January–August of year y−1y-1;

  • •

    calibration: September of year y−1y-1–April of year yy;

  • •

    testing: May–December of year yy.

Each split contains eight months. Advancing the window by twelve months produces twelve evaluation windows and 9696 distinct test months. The miscoverage level is α=0.20\alpha=0.20 throughout.

Let Nt​jN_{tj} denote the installation count at station jj in month tt, and let ℐytr\mathcal{I}_{y}^{\mathrm{tr}} be the training months for year yy. We define the station-specific threshold τj,y\tau_{j,y}, the smoothed overload-loss coefficient ct​j(y)c_{tj}^{(y)}, and the sigmoid function σ\sigma as follows:

τj,y\displaystyle\tau_{j,y} =18​∑t∈ℐytrNt​j,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{I}_{y}^{\mathrm{tr}}}N_{tj},
ct​j(y)\displaystyle c_{tj}^{(y)} =σ⁡(0.5​(Nt​j−τj,y)),\displaystyle=\sigma\!\left(0.5(N_{tj}-\tau_{j,y})\right),
σ⁡(a)\displaystyle\sigma(a) =11+exp⁡(−a).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-a)}.

Thus, each station’s threshold is determined by its training-period installation history, and larger installation counts yield larger loss coefficients. The same threshold is used to transform the training, calibration, and test observations within that window.

The point predictor is the historical mean of the transformed training costs:

c^j,y=18​∑t∈ℐytrct​j(y).\hat{c}_{j,y}=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{I}_{y}^{\mathrm{tr}}}c_{tj}^{(y)}.

This historical-mean setting uses the four station histories directly. Predictions and calibrated sets are held fixed over the eight test months and updated when the window advances.

Allocation Model and Regret

Before the monthly loss coefficients are observed, a planner allocates a divisible upgrade budget of two station-equivalents. An upgrade fraction uj∈[0,1]u_{j}\in[0,1] reduces station jj’s exposure by the same fraction, subject to ∑juj≤2\sum_{j}u_{j}\leq 2. Writing xj=1−ujx_{j}=1-u_{j} for the remaining exposure gives the linear allocation model

minx∈𝒳sol⁡ct⊤​x,\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{sol}}}c_{t}^{\top}x, (56)
𝒳sol={x∈[0,1]4:𝟏⊤​x≥2}.\displaystyle\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{sol}}=\{x\in[0,1]^{4}:\mathbf{1}^{\top}x\geq 2\}.

Here the window superscript on ctc_{t} is suppressed. The objective is a dimensionless smoothed overload loss, and realized regret is

Rt​(x)=ct⊤​x−minv∈𝒳sol⁡ct⊤​v.R_{t}(x)=c_{t}^{\top}x-\min_{v\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{sol}}}c_{t}^{\top}v.

The feasible region has the eleven vertices

𝒱sol={v∈{0,1}4:𝟏⊤​v≥2}.\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{sol}}=\{v\in\{0,1\}^{4}:\mathbf{1}^{\top}v\geq 2\}.

Nominal PTO optimizes the predicted loss over this region. Pure RR chooses a vertex, corresponding to full upgrades at selected stations, while Continuous RR permits fractional upgrades across stations.

Calibration and Refinement

Each method computes its score on the eight calibration months using the fixed training-period predictor. The conformal order-statistic index is

kα=⌈(8+1)​(1−0.20)⌉=8,k_{\alpha}=\left\lceil(8+1)(1-0.20)\right\rceil=8,

so the threshold is the largest of that method’s eight calibration scores. Pure and Continuous RR share the same SPO+ threshold and uncertainty set.

The Residual-ℓ2\ell_{2}, Box, and KNN–Ellipsoid baselines follow Appendix B.7. For this historical-mean setting, their context input is constant and the calibrated sets are used over ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}. KNN uses all eight training observations, k=min⁡(100,ntrain)=8k=\min(100,n_{\mathrm{train}})=8; its small-sample covariance uses an eigenvalue floor of 10−1210^{-12}. The score definitions and other baseline parameters are unchanged.

The eleven vertices are explicitly available, so we retain every active SPO+ piece identified by the screening rule. A fixed-piece LP evaluates the worst-case regret of each candidate decision. Pure RR compares all eleven feasible vertices. Continuous RR combines the dual representations of all active pieces into the finite LP of Proposition 4, and its returned decision is evaluated again using the primal fixed-piece oracles. The master objective and recomputed worst-case regret agree within 10−610^{-6}. Solver settings follow Appendix B.11.

Hindsight optimizer ties are resolved by minimizing predicted cost among the tied vertices, followed by a fixed vertex order. Among equally good Pure-RR candidates, the implementation first minimizes the predicted objective gap and then uses the same fixed order.

Decision Performance

All methods are evaluated on the same 9696 test months. We pool their monthly regrets to compute the mean, linearly interpolated Q95, and empirical CVaR95 using the definitions in Appendix B.2. For this sample size, the upper 5%5\% corresponds to 4.84.8 observations, so CVaR95 uses the four largest regrets and 0.80.8 of the fifth-largest regret, divided by 4.84.8.

Pure and Continuous RR are run consecutively and share the piece models constructed in the Pure stage; the table reports their separately recorded stage times.

In Table 9, Continuous RR reduces CVaR95 from 0.37180.3718 to 0.24640.2464, a 33.7%33.7\% reduction, with a 1.7%1.7\% increase in mean regret. It also lowers Q95 from 0.26060.2606 to 0.20590.2059 and attains the lowest tail regret among the six methods. Residual-ℓ2\ell_{2} RO produces a similar tail profile, while Pure RR preserves the nominal decisions and their mean regret.

In all 9696 test months, Continuous RR spreads the budget across all four stations, with station-level upgrade fractions ranging from 0.4930.493 to 0.5070.507. Nominal PTO and Pure RR fully upgrade two stations. The application therefore gives a direct allocation interpretation of the mean–tail trade-off.

C.2 Sparse Transportation Linear Programs

Network and Data Generation

The network has eight origins, eight destinations, and 3232 permitted shipping arcs, half of the 6464 possible origin–destination connections. We use five independent seeds, 4242–4646. For each seed, supply and demand vectors are drawn independently from Dirichlet⁡(2,…,2)\operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,\ldots,2) and then fixed, each summing to one. Draws are screened to keep distinct proper supply and demand subset sums more than 10−910^{-9} apart, giving nondegenerate transportation vertices.

To construct a feasible sparse network, we first solve the complete-network transportation problem with arc costs sampled independently from Unif⁡[0,1]\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]. We retain the resulting spanning-tree support of fifteen arcs and add seventeen arcs sampled without replacement from the remaining connections. The resulting arc set, supply vector, and demand vector are shared by all training, calibration, and test observations for that seed.

We use the quadratic multiplicative-noise generator from Appendix B.1. For each arc ee, let θe\theta_{e} denote its feature-coefficient vector, μe​(Z)\mu_{e}(Z) its conditional mean cost, and ξe\xi_{e} its multiplicative noise:

Z\displaystyle Z ∼Unif⁡([0,4]15),\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,4]^{15}),
μe​(Z)\displaystyle\mu_{e}(Z) =(θe⊤​Z)2,\displaystyle=(\theta_{e}^{\top}Z)^{2},
Ce\displaystyle C_{e} =μe​(Z)​ξe,ξe​∼iid​Unif⁡[0.8,1.2].\displaystyle=\mu_{e}(Z)\xi_{e},\qquad\xi_{e}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}[0.8,1.2].

For the first thirteen features, the coefficients satisfy

θe​ℓ\displaystyle\theta_{e\ell} =De​ℓ​Ae​ℓ,\displaystyle=D_{e\ell}A_{e\ell},
De​ℓ\displaystyle D_{e\ell} ∼Bernoulli⁡(0.5),\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.5),
Ae​ℓ\displaystyle A_{e\ell} ∼Unif⁡[0.8,1.2],\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0.8,1.2],

independently across arcs and features; the final two coefficients are zero. The signal matrix is generated once per seed and held fixed across the three data splits. Contexts and multiplicative noises are independent across observations. Costs are nonnegative and are used directly as minimization coefficients.

Transportation Model

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} be the set of permitted arcs. For e=(i,j)∈ℰe=(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}, let xi​jx_{ij} denote the shipment from origin ii to destination jj and ci​jc_{ij} its realized unit cost. With supplies aia_{i} and demands bjb_{j}, the transportation LP is:

minx≥0\displaystyle\min_{x\geq 0} ∑(i,j)∈ℰci​j​xi​j,\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}c_{ij}x_{ij}, (57)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} ∑j:(i,j)∈ℰxi​j=ai,i=1,…,8,\displaystyle\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}x_{ij}=a_{i},\quad i=1,\ldots,8,
∑i:(i,j)∈ℰxi​j=bj,j=1,…,8.\displaystyle\sum_{i:(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}x_{ij}=b_{j},\quad j=1,\ldots,8.

Total shipment volume is one. Removing one redundant demand equality gives the standard form

𝒳tr={x∈ℝ+32:A​x=h},A∈ℝ15×32,\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{32}:Ax=h\},\qquad A\in\mathbb{R}^{15\times 32},

where AA is the balance-constraint matrix of rank 1515 and h∈ℝ15h\in\mathbb{R}^{15} contains the eight supplies and seven retained demands. The feasible region has dimension 1717. Each nondegenerate vertex has fifteen positive arcs forming a spanning tree. Pure RR selects such a vertex; Continuous RR allows any feasible shipment plan. For a realized arc-cost vector cc, regret is

R⁡(x,c)=c⊤​x−minv∈𝒳tr⁡c⊤​v.R(x;c)=c^{\top}x-\min_{v\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{tr}}}c^{\top}v.

Prediction and Calibration

Each seed uses 50005000 training observations, 20002000 calibration observations, and 500500 test observations. All six methods share these observations and sample splits. The predictor is multi-output polynomial kernel ridge regression with the kernel, tuning grid, and training-only five-fold selection procedure of Appendix B.7. Feature and target standardization are fitted within each training fold. All five seeds select degree 22 and λ=2.154\lambda=2.154, after which the model is refitted on all 50005000 training observations. Predicted costs are returned to the original scale and clipped below at zero.

We use α=0.10\alpha=0.10. Each score has its own threshold, given by order statistic

kα=⌈(2000+1)​(1−0.10)⌉=1801k_{\alpha}=\left\lceil(2000+1)(1-0.10)\right\rceil=1801

of its calibration scores. Both SPO+ refinements use the same SPO+ scores and threshold. The Residual-ℓ2\ell_{2}, Box, and KNN–Ellipsoid baselines follow Appendix B.7, with the known support c≥0c\geq 0 replacing the knapsack sign constraint. Their score definitions, training procedures, and hyperparameters, including k=100k=100 for KNN, are unchanged.

Active-Piece Generation and Refinement

Active pieces are generated from the nominal transportation vertex in nondecreasing predicted-gap order. The adjacency oracle adds a nonbasic arc to the current spanning tree, follows the resulting cycle, and adjusts alternating flows until one tree arc leaves the support. Positive-arc supports identify distinct vertices. As in the knapsack experiment, only vertices satisfying the active-piece screening condition are expanded.

The generator uses requested prefix budgets

M∈{1,5,10,25,50,100,200},M\in\{1,5,10,25,50,100,200\},

extending through a complete equal-gap plateau when needed. Each retained piece supplies a fixed-piece LP adversary with c≥0c\geq 0. Continuous RR uses an LP master with scenario cuts. Pure RR uses the same cuts and binary arc-selection variables yi​jy_{ij} to represent a transportation vertex:

0≤xi​j\displaystyle 0\leq x_{ij} ≤min⁡(ai,bj)​yi​j,\displaystyle\leq\min(a_{i},b_{j})y_{ij},
∑(i,j)∈ℰyi​j\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}y_{ij} ≤15,yi​j∈{0,1},\displaystyle\leq 15,\qquad y_{ij}\in\{0,1\},

together with the balance constraints in (57). Thus Pure RR ranges over all transportation vertices and Continuous RR over the full feasible polytope; the prefix restricts the adversarial pieces.

Let LB\mathrm{LB} denote the master lower bound and UB\mathrm{UB} the full-problem upper bound obtained by combining the adversarial upper bound with the omitted-piece bound in Corollary 1. Refinement stops when UB−LB\mathrm{UB}-\mathrm{LB} is at most

10−6​max⁡{1,|LB|,|UB|},10^{-6}\max\{1,|\mathrm{LB}|,|\mathrm{UB}|\},

or the final prefix budget is reached. The constraint-generation loops have per-instance time budgets of 3030 seconds for Pure RR and 2020 seconds for Continuous RR. Solver settings follow Appendix B.11, with feasibility and integrality tolerances of 10−910^{-9} for the pure master. Nominal and hindsight LPs use deterministic dual simplex and a fixed secondary objective to resolve optimizer ties.

At the final budget, Pure RR is certified on all 25002500 test instances and Continuous RR on 24932493 of 25002500; neither method reaches its time budget. The performance summaries include the returned feasible decisions for all 500500 test instances per seed.

Decision Performance

For each seed, we compute mean regret, Q95, CVaR95, the decision-change rate, and mean online time over its 500500 test observations. Table 10 reports the arithmetic mean of these per-seed summaries over the five seeds. Time includes amortized prediction and baseline-query costs together with optimization, excluding offline training and calibration. Pure and Continuous RR run consecutively within each generation round, sharing active-piece search and model construction; their reported times include this common work and their respective optimization stages.

Continuous RR reduces Q95 from 3.7203.720 to 3.4663.466 and CVaR95 from 5.3795.379 to 4.8754.875, a 9.4%9.4\% reduction in CVaR95, while mean regret increases from 0.8430.843 to 1.2351.235. Pure RR remains close to nominal average performance and has the lowest mean regret among the robust methods. It changes 6.96%6.96\% of nominal shipment plans, illustrating selective intervention under coupled supply and demand constraints.
